extracted.intended_audience: scholars of higher education, program officers, grant-panelists, and researchers interested in peer review and disciplinary evaluation cultures
extracted.subtask_description: Describes how disciplinary cultures shape standards used to evaluate grant proposals on multidisciplinary panels, and the informal rules panelists use to reach consensus across epistemological divides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of cognitive contextualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists use the criteria of evaluation most appropriate to the field or discipline of the proposal under review; different standards should be applied to different disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called explicitly the 'rule of cognitive contextualization.' Panelists recognize disciplinary differences and are expected to evaluate proposals using the standards of the discipline relevant to the proposal, rather than imposing a single universal standard across fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good craftsmanship in empirical research (history)
rubrics_metrics.description: History's consensus about excellence is based on a shared definition of good craftsmanship in the practice of empirical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historians emphasize empirical methods, contextual knowledge, and craftsmanship; broad agreement about these practices facilitates panel consensus in history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formalization / theoretical rigor (economics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Economists' consensus results from cognitive consolidation around mathematical tools and formalization; excellence is often seen as an intrinsic property of ideas discovered through formal methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economists tend to view evaluation as a straightforward separation of winners and losers, downplaying intersubjectivity; they prioritize formal/theoretical clarity and the discovery of 'ideas that are valuable' that change understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual knowledge and linguistic competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether applicants have sufficient contextual expertise (including language skills) necessary for the proposed country/area studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some disciplines (e.g., history, area studies) treat lack of language familiarity as a substantive deficiency; other disciplines (e.g., some economists) may view such objections as less relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and significance (contested in some fields, especially English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of originality and significance are disputed in certain disciplines, leading to low consensus on what constitutes excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disciplines like English, panelists report a proliferation of criteria and skepticism about universal standards; what counts as originality/significance may be seen as relative to interpretive communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for ideological and methodological pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to tolerate and adjudicate among multiple methodologies and ideological perspectives is itself a possible marker of disciplinary maturity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An alternative view of maturity suggests fields that accept pluralism (methodological/ideological) are more advanced; panels may value pluralist openness in evaluating interdisciplinary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of theory and politics as evaluative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of theoretical commitments and political orientations as bases for assessing proposals; theory can be divisive within disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disciplines such as English and history, disputes over theory and politics affect judgments of significance and originality and can limit consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological positions, politics, and method (anthropology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropology places particular weight on epistemological stances, political commitments, and methodological choices when distinguishing worthy cultural analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthropologists engage in boundary work to separate what counts as adequate cultural analysis, making epistemology and method central evaluative criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for quantitative versus qualitative methods
rubrics_metrics.description: In some fields (e.g., political science) internal conflicts arise over privileging quantitative methods over qualitative approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methodological hierarchies shape standards of evaluation within a discipline and influence which proposals are favored on panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific matrices for measuring significance/originality (philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some fields (notably philosophy) insist on traditional, discipline-specific matrices to judge significance and originality and often believe only insiders can appropriately evaluate work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers may be inward-looking and claim specialized criteria are necessary; outsiders may view this as elitist or exclusionary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivist versus intersubjective conceptions of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Tension between viewing excellence as an intrinsic property of the object (objectivist) versus a negotiated, intersubjective definition arrived at by panelists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economists are characterized as more objectivist (excellence resides in the proposal/project), while historians and literary scholars more often see excellence as negotiated among evaluators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program officer promotion of pluralism and panel culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers can foster a culture of pluralism to counterbalance disciplinary differences and help panels reach shared commitments to academic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active promotion of pluralism by administrators is a procedural mechanism by which panels are steered toward compromise and mutual respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural constraints that shape evaluation (time, rules, need for consensus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules and exigencies of reviewing—limited time and requirement to make funding decisions—push panelists toward agreement and shape evaluative outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical constraints of peer review (meeting time, decision deadlines) channel deliberations and may privilege criteria that enable quicker consensus-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpersonal norms: willingness to listen and defer to expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel success depends on members' willingness to listen to others and defer to disciplinary experts when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference and attentiveness help panels bridge epistemological divides; hearing specialists explain their perspectives can turn reviewing into a learning experience for non-specialists.
